newsitem.title: USA: Gov. Whitman's budget gets generally good reviews.
newsitem.headline: Gov. Whitman's budget gets generally good reviews.

text.p: Gov. Christie Whitman on Wednesday outlined a spending plan for New Jersey in the fiscal year starting July 1.
While spending is rising only 1.3 percent, the budget contains small initiatives designed to please key constituencies.
Bond raters thought the budget appreared reasonable.

Steven Hochman, assistant director of state ratings at Moody's Investors Service, said, "The economic assumptions appear to be reasonable. Their revenues to date in the current fiscal year are on target."
And the revenue projections for the next fiscal year appear to be reasonable, Hochman said.
However, he noted, "We have questions about the non-recurring resources."
He cited the projected benefits of the proposed pension obligation bond program and the potential for budget relief.
"That is an area we will be examining more closely," he said. Moody's rates the state's general obligation bonds Aa1.
Robin Prunty, a director with Standard & Poor's Corp, said the pension financing plan "in and of itself" would not cause the state's rating to be downgraded. S&P rates the debt AA-plus.
She also added, "We are comfortable with thier use of non-recurring revenues."
Environmentalists were pleased that the Department of Environmental Protection will not lose any staff positions in the 1,235 job cuts she announced.
Curtis Fisher of the New Jersey Public Interest Reasearch Group said he was pleased by a pilot project to operate 50 buses fueled by natural gas.
Child advocates were pleased by her proposed health insurance plan for children who lack coverage. Children First will be a private-public partnership, Whitman said.
The utility industry was pleased by her plan to end the Gross Receipts and Franchise Tax, but mayors and municipal managers were wary about the impact on state aid.

Whitman defended the sale of $3.4 billion in bonds to liquidate unfunded liabilities in four state pension plans. That will enable Treasurer Brian Clymer to divert some of $2.3 billion in surplus cash in those funds to defray parts of the state's annual contributions.
Total expenditures will reach $16.4 billion, up from a revised FY 1997 total of $16.2 billion.

The budget deals some bad news to local governments and to higher education -- state aid will remain the same. It also calls for shedding 1,235 jobs, with an estimated 735 by layoff. Clymer said that if historic patterns hold up, actual layoffs will be about 320.
The budget relies on two controversial gimmicks to achieve a comnfortable balance.

One would raise $200 million by selling the state's temporary disability insurance plan, which covers 2.4 million New Jerseyans with a $105 payroll tax. "Private firms already provide this insurance just as efficiently," Whitman said.

The second maneuver would have a bigger impact. It would raise $3.4 billion by the sale of bonds to liquidate the unfunded liabilities in the four pension fdunds run on behalf of state, county and local employees. That would free up $2.3 billion in "surplus" -- capital not needed to cover current obligations.

Clymer proposes to use some of those funds to reduce the state's cash contribution to the funds by $269 million in the current budget and $354 million in the next. He said Wall Street has no objection, since it is merely an exchange of one form of debt for another.
--U.S. Municipal Desk, 212-859-1650
